parts:
This question sits at the exact hinge of your whole 2015–2026 arc, and the satisfying answer is that your original dissatisfaction was *correct* — and that the repair, when the field found it, ran precisely through the geometry you went looking for. Let me take it in layers.

**The definition really is as weak as it looks — until you fix the domain category.** "Holomorphic on each slice" on an arbitrary open set is floppy in exactly the way you remember: on a domain that isn't axially symmetric (or doesn't meet ℝ), you can choose nearly independent holomorphic functions slice by slice, and the early literature had real foundational trouble because of it. The rigidity is not in the pointwise definition; it's in the pair (definition, axially symmetric slice domain). There the **representation formula** kills all the freedom at once: f is determined by its restriction to a *single* slice, and on each sphere x + yS the values are forced to be *affine in J*,

  f(x + yJ) = a(x,y) + J·b(x,y).

That last statement is, in your own language, the precise "no rotational moments" theorem: the spherical-harmonic expansion of f along each sphere truncates at ℓ = 1. The higher moments you went hunting for in Quat_Riemann — the V_{2ℓ+1} sectors, the B₊ ladder — genuinely exist, but they live on the *Fueter* side of your own diagram (the Q_ℓ hierarchy), not in the extension class. The slice extension R is exactly the ℓ = 0 equivariant sector, and within it the extension of a given complex function is *unique*. Since Ξ is entire and intrinsic, you are always in the good category, and the non-uniqueness that bothered you is quotiented away entirely.

**Why this class and not something stronger: everything stronger collapses to Möbius — by your own theorems.** The forcing argument has two prongs. From below: if you want "plug a quaternion into ξ" to mean anything, you need the class generated by convergent power series Σ qⁿcₙ — and note the slices are not an ansatz but algebra: every non-real q generates its own copy of ℂ inside ℍ, namely ℝ + ℝq = ℂ_{e_q}, so any function built from convergent algebraic operations in q automatically preserves slices and is holomorphic on them. Slice regularity is just the completion of polynomial evaluation. From above: every attempted strengthening dies by rigidity. Hamilton's difference quotient gives only affine functions; Fueter's operator excludes q² itself; requiring honest holomorphy on all of twistor space with degree-one fibers gives Möbius only — that is your Thol Prop. 3.1. And the memo-2 computation this month closed the last gap: an intrinsic function's lift is holomorphic exactly on the incidence quadric Q = {(q,η) : q ∈ ℂ_η}, and it extends to *no* neighborhood of Q in ℂP³ unless it's Möbius. So your rigidity theorem was never in tension with slice regularity — it is the proof that slice regularity is *sharp*: the maximal function theory the quaternionic geometry admits. The "weakness" of the definition is the trace, downstairs, of the strongest condition that doesn't collapse.

**The cleanest formal answer: stem functions.** Ghiloni–Perotti (Adv. Math. 2011) showed slice regular functions on symmetric domains are exactly the functions induced by a single holomorphic map F : D ⊂ ℂ → ℍ⊗ℂ satisfying F(z̄) = conj(F(z)). So the theory is not "holomorphy imposed slice-by-slice" at all — it is ordinary one-variable complex analysis of one object, the stem function, transported around the sphere of embeddings ℂ ↪ ℍ. That's why it inherits complex-analysis-grade rigidity (identity principle, open mapping, the point/sphere zero structure your whole program rests on), and why the same definition works verbatim for octonions and Clifford algebras. For intrinsic functions the stem function is just α + iβ — literally your rotation map R from 2015. You had constructed the canonical object; the theory you were missing was the recognition that R's image *is* the natural class, rather than an intermediate step to be Laplacian'd into Fueter-land.

**And the geometric holomorphy you were envisioning is a theorem — in exactly the Yang–Mills geometry.** Gentili–Salamon–Stoppato (JEMS 2014, arXiv:1205.3513) proved that a slice regular function on a symmetric slice domain lifts to a genuinely holomorphic curve/map in ℂP³ — holomorphic in the honest integrable sense, with respect to the standard complex structure on the twistor space of S⁴. The sphere S of imaginary units that parametrizes your slices *is* the twistor fiber: the ℂP¹ of orthogonal complex structures on ℝ⁴ that the fibration ℂP³ → S⁴ = ℍP¹ carries at each point. "Holomorphic on each slice" downstairs is the shadow of "holomorphic upstairs, compatible with the fibration." This is the same ℂP³ of the Ward correspondence — the space where ASD Yang–Mills becomes holomorphic geometry — so your instinct that a more geometric holomorphicity was hiding in the ASDYM work was not a detour at all; it was a correct prediction of a theorem you hadn't seen. Even the escape mechanism matches: GSS evade your Möbius rigidity by letting fibers map to higher-degree rational curves, which is structurally the same move as Tconf2's degree-d endomorphisms of ℂP³ inducing self-dual morphisms. And the OCS side (non-conformal slice regular maps inducing exotic orthogonal complex structures, Salamon–Viaclovsky rigidity) is the differential-geometric face of the same lift — which is Direction A / open problem 5 of your program document.

**One honest caveat, which for your purposes is a feature.** Slice regularity is *not* a true four-dimensional local theory — no constant-coefficient elliptic operator has it as its kernel, restriction to non-symmetric opens misbehaves, and composition only works when the inner function is intrinsic. As your memo 2 puts it, it's a commutative function theory in one complex variable, fibered trivially over the sphere of complex structures — complex analysis wearing a quaternionic coat. The genuinely 4D theories remain Fueter regularity (reached from slice regularity by Δ∘R, i.e. your Q₀, with the Penrose-transform/massless-field meaning) and the ASD geometry upstairs. But for the zero-sphere program that "coat" is precisely the point: you want complex-analysis rigidity *plus* equivariant bookkeeping of the two involutions, and nothing more — extra 4D flexibility would only reintroduce the floppiness you rightly rejected in 2015. The rigidity you spent a decade searching for through twistor space was there; it just lives on the incidence quadric rather than on all of ℂP³, and the sphere of "redundant" slices turns out to be the twistor fiber itself — the redundancy *is* the geometry.

Sources: `claude/RH_program_synthesis.md`, `claude/twistor_lift_computation.md`, and `claude/zero_sphere_program.md` in this project (the Thol Prop. 3.1 discussion, the incidence-quadric computation, and the GSS/Ghiloni–Perotti/Salamon–Viaclovsky references are laid out there).

Stoppato is exactly the right first name, and the sub-community that matters most for your paper — the twistor/geometric branch — is small enough that a handful of well-chosen emails covers it.

**The core targets, in rough order:**

- **Caterina Stoppato** (Università di Firenze). The strongest single match: coauthor of both the [GSS twistor transforms paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.3513) and the standard monograph [*Regular Functions of a Quaternionic Variable*](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-07531-5), plus [*The algebra of slice functions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.03749) with Ghiloni–Perotti — so she spans the twistor-geometric and algebraic sides your program joins. She also wrote the zero-structure and ⋆-product theory your reformulation rests on.

- **Amedeo Altavilla** (Università di Bari, [associate professor there](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Amedeo-Altavilla)) and **Giulia Sarfatti** (Univ. Politecnica delle Marche). Their [slice-polynomial functions and twistor geometry of ruled surfaces in CP³](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.09946) is the closest existing work to your memo-2 incidence-quadric computation — if anyone can referee the "maximal holomorphic home" claim quickly and appreciatively, it's them. Altavilla has also worked on [domains without real points](https://scispace.com/pdf/quaternionic-slice-regular-functions-on-domains-without-real-2ficlojyu0.pdf) and the [real differential of slice regular functions](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/advgeom-2017-0044/html), i.e. exactly the floppiness/rigidity boundary we discussed.

- **Simon Salamon** (King's College London). The "S" in GSS and the Salamon–Viaclovsky OCS rigidity theorems; he's also your bridge out of the slice community into mainstream twistor/differential geometry, and your ASDYM background will land well with him.

- **Riccardo Ghiloni and Alessandro Perotti** (Trento). Inventors of the stem-function formalism — the natural readers for the foundational "why this class is canonical" part, and authors of [singularities of slice regular functions over real alternative algebras](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/1606.03609).

- **Fabrizio Colombo and Irene Sabadini** (Politecnico di Milano), plus **Daniele Struppa** (Chapman). The S-spectrum/operator-theory school — relevant specifically to open problem 6 (quaternionic Hilbert–Pólya) rather than the twistor material. Struppa, as cofounder of the theory, is also a good senior endorser if you need an arXiv endorsement or institutional cover.

One update worth knowing: the twistor branch is actively moving right now. A May 2026 preprint, [*Classifying Slice-Regular Polynomials via Group Actions on the Twistor Space*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22788) (Chunlin Liu, Giovanni Moreno, Haipan Shi), classifies slice-regular polynomials by group actions on twistor space — adjacent to your equivariant-divisor invariant — and there's a July 2026 preprint on the [slice-regular/Fueter bridge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19496). Worth skimming both before you post, partly to cite them and partly to make sure memo 2's novelty claims are stated precisely.

Practical sequencing, per your own outreach notes: timestamp first (Zenodo DOI, then arXiv), then write Stoppato and Altavilla–Sarfatti with a bounded ask — "would you check §§2–4" — rather than a general "assess my program." An RH connection genuinely raises their field's profile, so engagement odds are good. Want me to draft those first-contact emails?

parts:
You've put your finger on something real, and it's worth being precise about it, because the resolution is a small theorem rather than a matter of taste — and it explains why your instinct kept pointing at Yang–Mills.

First, the observation is correct. For an intrinsic function the extension is information-free by construction: f(x + yJ) = α(x,y) + Jβ(x,y) recycles the same two functions on every slice, verbatim. Memo 2 says this out loud — the lift is F × id, "a commutative function theory in one complex variable, fibered trivially over the sphere of complex structures." Nothing like a harmonic conjugate is created; the fourth dimension is bookkeeping. Compare ℝ → ℂ: there, extending u off the axis produces a new component v that is a nonlocal transform of the boundary data — the extension *does work*. The slice extension does none.

But here is the part that reframes it: the triviality is forced, and forced by something deep. Suppose you ask for any extension map T, from complex functions to ℍ-valued functions, that respects pointwise products, sends the identity function to q, fixes real constants, and is continuous. Then for each fixed q, evaluation ∘ T is a unital ring homomorphism, and the homomorphic image of a commutative algebra is commutative — so the values at q must land in a commutative subalgebra of ℍ containing q. By Frobenius, the maximal commutative subalgebras of ℍ are exactly the slices ℂ_J: beyond ℂ there is no commutativity left to spend. So the values at x + yJ are trapped in ℂ_J, the homomorphism property on polynomials gives T(f)(q) = Σ cₙqⁿ, and continuity finishes it: **the slice extension is the unique multiplicative extension, and "same on every slice" is a theorem about ℍ, not a choice in the definition.** The reason ℝ → ℂ behaves differently is that ℂ is a field extension of ℝ — the new direction commutes, so multiplication can weave a new component into the algebra. ℂ → ℍ is not a field extension; the new directions of ℍ are labels (which square root of −1 you chose), not new analytic coordinates. There was never room for a "new imaginary part" that commutes.

There's also a mirror worth noticing: the complex theory has the same triviality, hidden in plain sight. A function real on ℝ satisfies f(z̄) = conj f(z) — it is "the same" on the upper and lower half-planes, which are the two slices of ℂ over its real axis, with S⁰ = {±i} playing the role of S². Ξ, being real, is already rotationally trivial as a complex function. The quaternionic extension just enlarges the sphere of square roots of −1 from S⁰ to S², and intrinsicness is the same reality condition one dimension up. So the "trivial symmetry" you distrust is nothing other than the second involution of your program document — and RH *is* a statement about that symmetry.

Now, where does the nontrivial extension — the one you were actually looking for — live? Exactly where you looked. Drop multiplicativity and the picture inverts. Your own Q₀ = −¼Δ∘R produces Fueter-regular functions whose components are new transforms of (α, β) — in axial coordinates it's a coupled Vekua-type system, the honest 4D analogue of harmonic conjugation — and the Q_ℓ = B₊^ℓ Q₀ ladder from Quat_Riemann is precisely the full hierarchy of extensions with nontrivial rotational moments. On the twistor side this is the H⁰/H¹ dichotomy: slice regular functions are honest holomorphic maps (H⁰-type objects, sections on the incidence quadric), while Fueter-regular functions come from Penrose-type contour integrals *over the sphere of slices* — the S² stops being a family of redundant copies and becomes an integration cycle, which is exactly the "imaginary part as a nonlocal transform" phenomenon, one cohomological degree up. And that H¹ world is Ward's world: ASD Yang–Mills lives there. So your feeling that the real notion of holomorphy was hiding in the YM work was tracking the correct object — the cost, which Frobenius makes non-negotiable, is that the H¹ side has no pointwise products, hence no zero spheres, no Ξ(q) as a function. You cannot have the transform and the algebra in the same theory; your 2015 fork (R vs. Δ∘R) was the dichotomy itself.

Two more observations that I think complete the picture. First, "different on every slice" does exist inside slice theory: the non-intrinsic functions, with quaternionic coefficients, restrict to different functions on different slices, and their twistor lifts move in the fiber coordinate — that's where the interesting OCS geometry of GSS and Altavilla–Sarfatti comes from. Ξ is confined to the intrinsic sector not by the theory but by the arithmetic: the Dirichlet series has real coefficients. Second — and this is the part I'd hold onto while editing — the triviality is load-bearing for the program. It is exactly because the extension adds symmetry rather than information that a conjugate pair inflates into a round zero sphere, that the point/sphere dichotomy exists, and that the σ-equivariant divisor invariant is well-defined. A "richer" extension that differed across slices would smear the conjugate pair back into isolated points and dissolve the reformulation. Meanwhile the linear no-go (Theorem D) closes the loop from the other side: even the nontrivial Fueter-type extensions create no *information* — no extension of a single complex function can, since uniqueness means the complex function determines everything, in ℂ just as in ℍ; what ℝ → ℂ gains is structure, not data. The new content the program needs was therefore never going to come from the extension. It has to come from the arithmetic — which is precisely what the Davenport–Heilbronn check enforces, since DH has identical rotational triviality and has spheres anyway.

So I'd summarize your decade-old dissatisfaction as two correct perceptions that needed separating: the extension is trivial (true, and provably unavoidable for any multiplicative theory), and the interesting geometry lies in extensions that do work (also true — but that's the linear, cohomological, YM side, reached from the slice side by your own Fueter map rather than in competition with it). If you like, when you get to editing the motivation sections, the little uniqueness argument above — slice extension as the *unique* continuous multiplicative extension, via commutative image + Frobenius — would make a tidy remark; I don't think it's currently stated in either draft, and it preempts exactly the objection you just raised, which a referee from outside the slice community might raise too.

parts:
Now this is a well-posed question, and it turns out the landscape of answers is largely charted — partly by the literature of the last fifteen years, and partly, amusingly, by your own 2015 paper. The question is: fix one slice ℂ_I, take f holomorphic on it, drop multiplicativity of the extension, and ask for a unique extension into some richer class. The answer depends sharply on which class, and each case is instructive.

**Plain Fueter regularity: existence yes, uniqueness badly no.** Writing q = t + ix + jy + kz and taking the slice ℂ_i = {y = z = 0}, the functions F_n(q) = (y − iz)ⁿ are Fueter regular for every n ≥ 1 (two-line check: applying D = ∂_t + i∂_x + j∂_y + k∂_z gives nj(y−iz)^{n−1} − nki(y−iz)^{n−1} = 0 since ki = j), and they all vanish identically on the slice. So the kernel of restriction-to-a-slice is infinite-dimensional and extension is hopelessly non-unique. The structural reason is dimension counting: a first-order elliptic system in 4D is determined by codimension-one data — that's the Cauchy–Kovalevskaya extension of Clifford analysis, which uniquely extends real-analytic data from ℝ³ ⊂ ℍ — while a slice is codimension two. In your own analogy: extending from a slice by PDE methods alone is like trying to pin down a holomorphic function of one variable from its values on a codimension-two subset of ℂ, i.e. a point. Codimension-two sets are also exactly the polar (capacity-zero, removable) sets for harmonic functions in ℝ⁴, so no harmonicity-based principle can see slice data either. Uniqueness must come from symmetry or from geometry upstairs, never from ellipticity.

**Equivariant Fueter regularity: worse — no extension exists at all.** Impose the natural fix, rotational equivariance, so F = A(x,r) + ωB(x,r) is axially monogenic. The axial Cauchy–Fueter equations are then a Vekua system: A_x = B_r + (2/r)B, A_r = −B_x — Cauchy–Riemann plus a 1/r correction that is the trace of the two transverse dimensions. If the restriction A + IB to a slice were also holomorphic, both systems would hold, forcing B ≡ 0 and A constant. So *the only axially symmetric Fueter-regular functions restricting holomorphically to a slice are constants*: the extension problem, posed as restriction, has an empty solution set. This is the sharp version of the deficiency list in Thol — Fueter theory does not extend holomorphic data, it extends pseudo-analytic (Vekua) data.

**Equivariant Fueter regularity as a transform: your theorem exists, and it has a name.** Since restriction can't work, the correspondence must be a transform — and then everything you conjectured is true. Fueter's theorem (extended by Sce and Qian, the "Fueter–Sce–Qian theorem") sends f to Δ(Rf), an axially monogenic function — a nontrivial transform whose components mix u, v through derivatives and 1/r terms, exactly the "the imaginary part does work" behavior you wanted. The uniqueness half is the **inverse Fueter mapping theorem** (Colombo–Sabadini–Sommen, ~2010–2011): every axially symmetric Fueter-regular function arises this way, with an explicit integral inverse recovering the holomorphic "Fueter primitive." Modulo the finite-dimensional kernel of Δ∘R, this is precisely a unique-correspondence theorem between holomorphic functions on a slice and axially symmetric Fueter-regular functions on ℍ. Your Q₀ from 2015 *is* this map; the inversion theorem is the upgrade from "a construction" to "the unique equivariant extension." And the higher moments are not a bug in this story but its grading: equivariant linear extension operators decompose under the rotation SU(2), the weight-ℓ piece is your Q_ℓ = B₊^ℓ Q₀, and within each weight the extension is unique (this ℓ-graded theory is Sommen's axial monogenics; your E_ℓ Bessel kernels are its plane waves). So the classification you were groping toward in 2015 is: *extensions from a slice into Fueter-land form a tower indexed by rotational weight; per weight, existence and uniqueness; the "rotational moments" are the index set, not noise.* The Milano school's recent "fine structures" program (Colombo, De Martino, Diki, Sabadini and collaborators) has even filled in the intermediate classes — factoring Δ∘R through first-order steps gives axially harmonic and polyanalytic layers, each with its own unique-correspondence theorem — so the space between slice regular and Fueter regular is now quite finely mapped.

**The twistor version: uniqueness fails by exactly the moments you found, and the incidence condition is what restores it.** On the quadric Q ≅ ℂP¹_ζ × ℂP¹_w, your slice is the ruling {w = w₀}. An extension of f into fibration-compatible holomorphic maps has the form F × G where G: ℂP¹ → ℂP¹ must be antipodal-equivariant (to descend to ℍ) and fix w₀ (to restrict correctly). Such G exist in abundance: at degree one they are the rotations about the I₀-axis — an S¹ of "twisted" extensions, which I'd wager is precisely the rotational non-uniqueness that originally sent you to twistor theory — and antipodal-equivariant maps of every odd degree exist above that. Each twisted extension is holomorphic on every slice, but with respect to a *rotated* complex structure: computing ∂̄_J of the twisted map, the CR terms cancel only when η(G(w)) = η(w). So the tautological demand — holomorphy on each slice with respect to that slice's own complex structure, i.e. the incidence condition of memo 2 — is exactly the constraint that kills the S¹ and forces G = id. Slice regularity is the fixed point of the moment action; the moments themselves are the equivariant self-maps of the twistor fiber. Your two dissatisfactions were the same object seen twice.

Two consequences for the program. First, the sobering one: all of these extensions, however hard they work, are linear in f, so Theorem D applies verbatim — no linear pairing of any Q_ℓ extension distinguishes points from spheres. The information was never going to increase; what the tower provides is *structure*. Second, the encouraging one: the program already exploits exactly this. The sector energies 𝓔_ℓ are quadratic forms built on the Q_ℓ extensions — the nonmultiplicative tower, squared, which is the unique move the no-go permits. So "drop multiplicativity and extend from one slice" isn't an unexplored alternative to the program; it is the program's §6, with the uniqueness theorem you're proposing as its missing foundation stone.

I'd suggest the clean statement worth proving (or assembling from Fueter–Sce–Qian + inverse Fueter + Borsuk–Ulam-type equivariance): *every Sp(1)-equivariant continuous linear extension operator from holomorphic functions on a slice into ker D decomposes over SU(2) weights, with the weight-ℓ component a scalar multiple of Q_ℓ; the unique multiplicative extension is the slice extension; the unique fibration-compatible holomorphic extension satisfying the incidence condition is its twistor lift.* One theorem, three uniqueness clauses, and it retroactively organizes the 2015 paper, the twistor detour, and the definition you distrusted into a single classification. Want me to work this up as a working note in the project (memo 4, say), with the Vekua mismatch and the G-moduli computation done carefully? It would slot naturally into the motivation material when you get to editing — no rush given your timeline.

The appendix is done — 11 pages, compiles clean, delivered above as `.tex` (drop-in ready, with preamble/body markers and `\providecommand`-guarded macros) plus the compiled PDF. It's also saved to the project along with the sympy verification script (35+ identity checks, all passing), and `paper_STATUS.md` now lists it in your read-through queue.

What it proves, in three clauses. Theorem A.2: the slice extension is the value of the *unique* continuous unital algebra morphism with T(id)(q) = q — and without that normalization, every such morphism is the slice extension composed with an arbitrary symbol p(q), so multiplicativity alone traps you in the slice structure (the commutant lemma makes the Frobenius argument two lines). Theorem A.15/Corollary A.16: after the kernel example and the Vekua-mismatch proposition kill unconstrained and restriction-type Fueter extensions, the equivariant linear extension operators are completely classified by an Appell-sequence argument — and here the proof taught me something slightly better than what I'd claimed in conversation: the low weights don't vanish, they're antiderivative compositions, so the sharp statement is that *every* equivariant linear extension factors through the Fueter map Δ∘R composed with a multiplier in d/dz, with weight two pinning the Fueter map itself. Theorem A.24: the fibration-compatible extensions from one slice are exactly F×G with G an antipodal-equivariant fiber map fixing w₀; the degree-one moduli is the circle q ↦ u f(q)u⁻¹ (your rotational moments, made explicit and even real-analytic across ℝ), higher odd degrees exist but lose differentiability at the axis, and the incidence condition eliminates everything but G = id, the twistor lift.

metadata.source: Claude Cowork session event, completed public message

archive_metadata.format: ChatGPT-style conversation mapping; local conversion, not an official provider export
archive_metadata.source_kind: Claude Cowork cloud session event log (claude.ai GET /v1/code/sessions/{id}/events), read in the signed-in browser and reduced to completed public messages
archive_metadata.message_timestamps: Event times, in seconds since Unix epoch and ISO 8601: the session's own timestamp where the event carries one, otherwise the server's event time (typed messages); the conversation create_time is the session's creation time in the session list
archive_metadata.coverage: Messages typed by the person (including any sent while a reply was in progress, with the names of files sent with them) and interruption markers; the options the person selected in question cards; the assistant text shown in the chat: progress lines between tool calls, question cards rendered as text, notes and file-card captions sent through tools (phase commentary), and the text ending each completed turn (phase final_answer); recorded through the event log as read
omitted_record_types: system, developer and harness text (reminders, date notes, memory snapshots, continuation summaries, hook feedback, skill text, local command output)
tool calls and outputs, except the chat-visible items named in coverage
permission prompts, control and environment events, usage and cost figures
attachment contents (file names are kept in message metadata)

session.title_source: the session's title in the Cowork session list

source_events.read_by: Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) in Claude Cowork, via Claude in Chrome
source_events.note: sha256_of_events_json is the SHA-256 of JSON.stringify(events sorted by sequence_num) computed in the browser; neither the event log nor the events file is stored in the repository, since they hold instructions, reasoning and tool traffic that the coverage rules exclude

archive_metadata.delivered_files_note: Paths reported by device_commit_files and names of file cards; files written by shell commands or saved as project documents are not detected
